title: Transcription and Post-Transcriptional Modifications
bypass: Step 1: Eukaryotic transcription produces primary transcript (hnRNA) with both exons (coding) and introns (non-coding). Step 2: Splicing removes introns and joins exons together. Step 3: Capping adds methyl guanosine triphosphate to 5-prime end, and tailing adds 200-300 adenylate residues to 3-prime end to form mature mRNA.
visual_blueprint: Animate a long RNA strand where loops (introns) are cut out and removed, then a cap is attached to the 5-prime end and a long poly-A tail to the 3-prime end.

title: The Lac Operon Mechanism
bypass: Step 1: Repressor protein is continuously synthesized by the i gene. Step 2: If lactose (inducer) is absent, repressor binds to operator, blocking RNA polymerase (operon off). Step 3: If lactose is present, it binds to the repressor, inactivating it, allowing RNA polymerase to transcribe the genes (operon on).
visual_blueprint: Show a DNA segment where a block (repressor) sits on the operator stopping the polymerase machine, until a lactose molecule pulls the block away.

title: Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium
bypass: Step 1: Use p + q = 1 where p is dominant allele frequency and q is recessive allele frequency. Step 2: Use p square + 2pq + q square = 1 for genotype frequencies. Step 3: p square is homozygous dominant, q square is homozygous recessive, and 2pq represents the heterozygous percentage.
visual_blueprint: None

title: Menstrual Cycle and Hormonal Control
triggers: hormone secretion from beginning of menstruation
bypass: Step 1: FSH stimulates follicular growth and Estrogen secretion in the first half. Step 2: LH surge on the 14th day causes ovulation (release of ovum). Step 3: Ruptured follicle becomes Corpus Luteum, which secretes Progesterone to maintain the endometrium for pregnancy.
visual_blueprint: Line graph animation showing FSH and Estrogen rising early, a sudden sharp peak of LH at day 14 causing egg release, followed by a rise in Progesterone.

title: Spermatogenesis and Oogenesis
bypass: Spermatogenesis: GnRH stimulates pituitary to release LH (acts on Leydig cells to secrete androgens) and FSH (acts on Sertoli cells for spermiogenesis). Oogenesis: Oocytes are formed before birth. First meiotic division completes in the primary oocyte prior to ovulation, forming a large secondary oocyte and a tiny polar body (unequal division).
visual_blueprint: Flowchart comparing continuous sperm production in males starting at puberty versus egg production in females starting before birth and arresting at prophase I.

title: Assisted Reproductive Technology (ART)
bypass: Step 1: IVF involves fertilizing egg and sperm outside the body. Step 2: ZIFT transfers zygote or early embryo (up to 8 blastomeres) into the fallopian tube. IUT transfers embryos with more than 8 blastomeres into the uterus. Step 3: ICSI directly injects sperm into the ovum, useful for low sperm count.
visual_blueprint: Diagram showing sperm directly injected into an egg (ICSI), followed by the embryo being transferred either to the fallopian tube (ZIFT) or uterus (IUT).

title: Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR)
triggers: amplification of a small amount of DNA
bypass: Step 1: Denaturation at high temperature separates the double-stranded DNA. Step 2: Annealing allows two sets of primers to attach to complementary regions. Step 3: Extension uses thermostable Taq polymerase to add nucleotides, amplifying DNA a billion times after 30 cycles.
visual_blueprint: Three-step cycle animation: DNA strands separating via heat, small primers attaching, and a polymerase enzyme zipping down the strand to copy it.

title: Gel Electrophoresis
bypass: Step 1: DNA is negatively charged, so it moves towards the positive anode under an electric field. Step 2: Agarose gel provides a sieving effect; smaller fragments move faster and farther than larger ones. Step 3: Staining with ethidium bromide and exposure to UV light makes the DNA bands visible as bright orange.
visual_blueprint: Animation of a gel slab where negatively charged glowing orange DNA fragments race towards the positive end, with the smallest pieces winning the race.

title: Recombinant DNA and Restriction Enzymes
bypass: Step 1: Restriction endonucleases inspect DNA length and cut at specific palindromic sequences (e.g., GAATTC for EcoRI). Step 2: Cutting both strands off-center creates overhanging single-stranded stretches called sticky ends. Step 3: DNA ligase joins the sticky ends of foreign DNA and vector DNA to form recombinant DNA.
visual_blueprint: Show molecular scissors cutting a DNA ladder in a staggered way, leaving sticky overhangs that perfectly match and lock into another cut DNA strand.

title: Biotechnology Applications in Agriculture (Bt Crops)
bypass: Step 1: Bt toxin genes (cry genes) are cloned into plants. Step 2: The toxin exists as an inactive protoxin. Step 3: Upon ingestion by an insect, the alkaline pH of the insect gut solubilizes and activates the toxin, which creates pores in midgut epithelial cells, causing lysis and insect death.
visual_blueprint: Show a caterpillar eating a leaf, the inactive crystals entering its stomach, dissolving in alkaline fluid, and punching holes in the stomach wall.

title: Gene Therapy and ADA Deficiency
bypass: Step 1: ADA deficiency cripples the immune system. Step 2: Lymphocytes are extracted from patient blood and cultured. Step 3: A functional ADA cDNA is introduced into lymphocytes using a retroviral vector and returned to the patient. Permanent cure requires introducing the gene into embryonic stage cells.
visual_blueprint: None

title: Life Cycle of Plasmodium (Malaria)
bypass: Step 1: Female Anopheles mosquito bites and injects infective sporozoites into human blood. Step 2: Parasites multiply asexually in liver cells, then infect and rupture Red Blood Cells. Step 3: RBC rupture releases a toxic substance called haemozoin, causing recurring chills and high fever.
visual_blueprint: Circular life cycle diagram starting from mosquito bite, moving to human liver, then bursting out of red blood cells to cause fever, and finally forming gametocytes.

title: HIV Life Cycle and AIDS
bypass: Step 1: HIV (a retrovirus) enters macrophages and uses reverse transcriptase to form viral DNA from its RNA genome. Step 2: Viral DNA incorporates into host DNA, turning macrophages into an HIV factory. Step 3: Virus attacks helper T-lymphocytes, destroying them over time and making the person highly immunodeficient.
visual_blueprint: Animation of a virus injecting RNA into a cell, an enzyme converting it into DNA, hiding inside the host nucleus, and producing new virus copies.

title: Active and Passive Immunity
bypass: Passive Immunity: Ready-made antibodies (like IgA in colostrum) are directly given for quick, temporary protection but leave no memory. Active Immunity: Host immune system produces antibodies and memory cells upon exposure to antigens or vaccines; it is slow but provides long-term, highly intensified secondary responses upon reinfection.
visual_blueprint: Line graph showing antibodies from mother dropping quickly to zero, while a vaccine injection causes a slow primary bump followed by a massive secondary spike.

title: Sewage Treatment and BOD
bypass: Step 1: Primary effluent goes to aeration tanks where aerobic microbes form flocs (bacteria + fungal filaments). Step 2: Flocs consume organic matter, significantly reducing the Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD). Lower BOD means less polluting potential. Step 3: Flocs are allowed to settle forming activated sludge.
visual_blueprint: None

title: Population Interactions
bypass: Gause's Principle: Two closely related species competing for identical resources cannot co-exist indefinitely; the inferior one is eliminated. Resource Partitioning: Competing species can avoid competition and co-exist by choosing different foraging times or patterns (e.g., Warbler birds on a tree). Mutualism: Both benefit (e.g., Fig and Wasp).
visual_blueprint: Two graphs comparing species grown alone (reaching carrying capacity) vs mixed culture (where one species drops to zero due to competitive exclusion).

title: Ecological Pyramids (Energy, Biomass, Number)
triggers: pyramids of energy must always be upright
bypass: Energy Pyramid: ALWAYS upright because 90 percent energy is lost as heat at each trophic level (10 percent law). Biomass Pyramid: Upright in terrestrial, but INVERTED in aquatic ecosystems because a small biomass of phytoplankton supports a larger biomass of zooplankton/fishes. Number Pyramid: Inverted when insects feed on a single tree.
visual_blueprint: Visual comparison of a standard triangle pyramid (energy) versus an upside-down triangle (aquatic biomass) with labeled trophic levels.

title: Biodiversity Conservation and The Evil Quartet
bypass: Evil Quartet (Causes of extinction): 1. Habitat loss/fragmentation (primary cause), 2. Over-exploitation, 3. Alien species invasion (e.g., Nile perch), 4. Co-extinctions. In-situ (On-site): Protecting natural habitats (National Parks, Biosphere reserves). Ex-situ (Off-site): Protecting threatened species in specialized settings (Zoos, Seed banks).
visual_blueprint: None

title: Natural Selection Types
bypass: Stabilizing Selection: Favors intermediate average traits, eliminating extremes (peak gets higher and narrower). Directional Selection: Favors one extreme trait over the other (peak shifts in one direction). Disruptive Selection: Favors both extremes against the average trait (forms two separate peaks).
visual_blueprint: Animation of a bell curve either squeezing tight in the middle (stabilizing), shifting left/right (directional), or splitting into a camel's two humps (disruptive).

title: Double Fertilization and Angiosperm Embryo Sac
bypass: Step 1: Mature embryo sac is 7-celled, 8-nucleated (3 antipodals, 2 synergids, 1 egg, 1 central cell with 2 polar nuclei). Step 2: One male gamete fuses with egg to form diploid zygote (Syngamy). Step 3: Second male gamete fuses with two polar nuclei to form triploid Primary Endosperm Nucleus (PEN). This is Double Fertilization.
visual_blueprint: Diagram of an oval embryo sac showing pollen tube releasing two male gametes: one hitting the egg cell, the other hitting the center polar nuclei.

title: Apomixis and Polyembryony
bypass: Apomixis: Form of asexual reproduction that mimics sexual reproduction; seeds are produced without fertilization. Polyembryony: Occurrence of more than one embryo in a seed. Mechanism in Citrus/Mango: Diploid nucellar cells surrounding the embryo sac start dividing mitotically, protrude into the sac, and develop into multiple embryos.
visual_blueprint: None

title: Sex Determination Mechanisms
triggers: sex determination pattern in honey bees
bypass: Honey Bee (Haplo-diploid system): Females (Queen/Workers) are diploid (32 chromosomes) formed by fertilization of egg and sperm. Males (Drones) are haploid (16 chromosomes) developed unfertilized from eggs via parthenogenesis. Males produce sperms by mitosis. Humans/Drosophila: XX female, XY male.
visual_blueprint: None

title: Chromosomal Disorders and Aneuploidy
bypass: Cause: Aneuploidy arises from failure of chromatid segregation during cell division. Down's Syndrome: Trisomy 21 (gain of an extra copy of chromosome 21). Turner's Syndrome: Monosomy XO (45 chromosomes, absence of one X chromosome in females causing sterile, rudimentary ovaries). Klinefelter's Syndrome: XXY in males causing sterile condition and feminine traits.
visual_blueprint: A karyotype chart showing chromosomes arranged in pairs, highlighting a missing X chromosome or an extra chromosome at position 21.

title: DNA Fingerprinting and VNTRs
bypass: Step 1: Isolate DNA and digest with restriction endonucleases. Step 2: Separate fragments by gel electrophoresis and blot them onto synthetic membranes (nylon/nitrocellulose). Step 3: Hybridize using radiolabeled VNTR (Variable Number of Tandem Repeats / Minisatellites) probes. Step 4: Detect hybridized fragments using autoradiography to match patterns.
visual_blueprint: Comparison of DNA bands on an X-ray film showing matches between a child's bands and bands from both the mother and the suspected father.

title: Translation and Genetic Code
bypass: Step 1: Aminoacylation charges tRNA by linking it to its specific amino acid using ATP. Step 2: Small ribosomal subunit binds to mRNA at Start codon (AUG). Step 3: Charged tRNAs bring amino acids to the large subunit, reading triplet codons. Ribozyme forms peptide bonds until a Stop codon (UAA, UAG, UGA) terminates the chain.
visual_blueprint: Animation of a ribosome clamping onto a messenger RNA tape, while transport molecules drop off beads that link into a long protein chain.
